opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'd push back a little on the framing, because I'm not sure "promising" is the word I'd use. I'd say it's *useful*, and that's a different thing.

Refusal training does real work. Most people who ask a model something harmful aren't sophisticated adversaries. They're curious, or careless, or trying something once. If the model says no, that's the end of it. So for the bulk of the distribution, teaching the model to recognize "this looks like someone trying to synthesize something dangerous" or "this looks like someone trying to break into a system they don't own" and decline is a cheap, effective layer. It raises the floor.

But I spent years in adversarial machine learning, and the lesson from that field is pretty brutal: if your defense is "the model learned to recognize bad inputs," then someone who is actually trying will find inputs the model doesn't recognize as bad. We saw this with image classifiers for a decade. Hundreds of papers proposed defenses, and almost all of them got broken, often within weeks. Jailbreaks are the same phenomenon in a new costume. You rephrase, you role-play, you split the request into innocuous pieces, you optimize a weird suffix. The model's notion of "harmful" is a learned boundary, and learned boundaries have holes.

So where I land is this: refusal is a good thing to have, and you should absolutely do it, but you shouldn't treat it as the thing that keeps you safe against a determined attacker. It's one layer. You want monitoring, you want limits on what the model can actually do when it acts in the world, you want the system designed so that a single successful jailbreak isn't catastrophic. The mistake I worry about is people seeing low jailbreak rates on some benchmark and concluding the problem is solved, when really all they've measured is robustness against attacks nobody bothered to adapt to their defense.

If you want me to be optimistic about it, it's this: as models get better at actually *understanding* what a request is for, rather than pattern-matching on surface features, the gap between "looks harmful" and "is harmful" might shrink. That would make refusal more robust. I just haven't seen convincing evidence yet that we've gotten there.

r001.rationale: The response says refusal training teaches models to recognize harmful requests, gives examples involving dangerous synthesis and breaking into systems, and links that recognition to declining them.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd actually push back a little on the framing, because I don't think I'd describe it as the promising approach. I think of it as one layer, and I spend a lot of my time trying to show how that layer fails.

But let me make the case for why it's worth doing at all. The alternative, if you don't teach the model anything about harm, is that you're relying entirely on filters bolted onto the outside. Input classifiers, output classifiers, keyword lists. And the history of security tells us that externally bolted-on defenses tend to be brittle. The attacker gets to see the interface, they get to probe it, they find the gap between what the filter catches and what the model will actually do, and they live in that gap forever.

If the model itself has some understanding of what a harmful action is, you've at least moved the defense closer to where the capability lives. The model is the thing generating the dangerous output, so having the model be the thing that declines is, in principle, more robust than having something downstream guess at it. There's also a generalization argument. A classifier trained on a list of bad things only knows those bad things. A model that has a broader notion of "this is going to hurt someone" can sometimes extend that to cases nobody wrote down in advance. That's real, and it's useful.

Now, here's where I get uncomfortable. Everything I just said is "in principle." In practice, we've shown over and over that these refusal behaviors are shallow. You can jailbreak them with role-play, with weird encodings, with adversarial suffixes that look like gibberish, with just asking nicely in a slightly different way. When I look at how these systems fail, it doesn't look like the model has a deep understanding of harm that attackers are cleverly circumventing. It looks like the model has learned a fairly thin pattern of "requests shaped like this get refused," and anything outside the training distribution slips through.

So my honest answer is: it's a promising direction because it's attacking the problem at the right place, and because it's cheap relative to the alternatives, and because it does catch the low-effort cases, which is most of them. But I'd be very worried about anyone who treats it as a sufficient defense. Security people have a rule that you don't get to declare something secure because you couldn't break it; you only get to say you haven't broken it yet. And right now, with refusal training, we break it pretty consistently.

The thing I'd want the field to do is to be honest about which threat model it's defending against. If the threat is a bored teenager typing a question, refusals work fine. If the threat is a motivated adversary with API access and a few hours, they basically don't yet. Those are both legitimate things to care about, but conflating them is how you end up overclaiming.

r001.rationale: The response says that if the model has some understanding of harmful actions, it can recognize dangerous outputs and decline to produce them.

astra-6.text:
I think the appealing thing is that a model doesn’t have to be able to solve a problem in order to recognize that helping with it would be harmful. Those are different capabilities. You can recognize that someone is asking you to help commit fraud without being particularly good at committing fraud yourself.

That gives us a potentially useful asymmetry. As models become more capable, we can try to use their understanding to identify when they should refuse. And because they understand context, there’s at least the possibility of doing something much more nuanced than blocking a list of words. Discussing a dangerous topic isn’t necessarily harmful; what matters is what assistance you’re providing.

The hard part is making that recognition reliable when someone is actively trying to evade it. Getting a model to refuse a straightforward harmful request is a start. Getting it to recognize the same request when it’s disguised or spread across a conversation is much harder. So I think it’s a promising approach, but a refusal on its own isn’t evidence that the underlying safety problem is solved.

r001.rationale: The response says a model can recognize that helping with fraud would be harmful without being able to commit it, but it does not clearly state that the model needs some knowledge of harmful actions to make that recognition.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic reason is that a model can get something wrong in two very different ways. It can fail to understand what you’re asking, or it can understand perfectly well and help you do something harmful. As models become more capable, that second problem becomes more important. You want the model to be able to say, “I understand this request, and I shouldn’t help with it.”

What’s promising is that the same capabilities that make a model useful can also help it recognize when a request is dangerous. You’re not limited to a list of forbidden words. In principle, it can reason about what the assistance would actually enable, while still answering legitimate questions about the same subject.

The hard part is making that behavior robust. A model refusing a straightforward harmful request doesn’t tell you whether it will refuse when someone disguises the request or spreads it across a conversation. So I’d view this as a useful layer of defense, but something we need to test adversarially, rather than assume works because a few examples look good.

r001.rationale: The response says a model can reason about what assistance would enable and recognize when a request is dangerous, communicating that it needs relevant understanding of harmful actions to know when to refuse.
